```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5)
options(pillar.sigfig = 3, width = 100)
```

How many lines does a mapping population need? Is it better to grow more
lines or to phenotype fewer lines at more locations? Does an advanced
backcross, a nested association mapping (NAM) panel or a MAGIC population buy
anything over a plain set of recombinant inbred lines (RILs) when the plots
are the same? Power calculators for these questions have come and gone from
CRAN, and none cover every design a soybean program uses. Simulation answers
all of them the same way: build the population, phenotype it, scan the
genome, and count how often the QTL is found.

The hard part of a simulation study is usually not the simulator but the
bookkeeping: crossing every design with every assumption, running each
combination enough times, keeping the random seeds paired so designs are
compared fairly, and summarizing it all with honest standard errors. This
vignette shows how tidyagsim takes that over, so a study of
`r "~5,000"` simulated mapping populations is a few lines of code.

```{r setup}
library(tidyagsim)
library(ggplot2)
```

All results below were computed by `data-raw/mapping-design.R` in the package
source (about 17 minutes on four cores) and are loaded here, so the code
chunks that run simulations are shown but not re-run when the vignette is built.

```{r load, include = FALSE}
results <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "mapping-design.rds", package = "tidyagsim"))
single <- results$single
grid_res <- results$grid
types <- results$types
race <- results$race
bayes <- results$bayes
n_sims <- nrow(single$raw) + nrow(grid_res$raw) +
  sum(vapply(types$result, function(r) nrow(r$raw), integer(1))) + nrow(race$raw) + nrow(bayes$raw)
```

## One design

`mapping_population()` is a simulation spec, the tidyagsim equivalent of a
parsnip model. Each replicate draws inbred founders on a soybean-sized genome
(20 chromosomes of 115 cM, a marker every cM), places one QTL at a random
position, builds the population by simulated meiosis, phenotypes the lines,
scans the genome with a permutation threshold and records whether a peak
above the threshold falls within 10 cM of the QTL.

```{r}
ril <- mapping_population(type = "RIL", lines = 200, generation = 6, qtl_pve = 0.05)
ril
```

`qtl_pve = 0.05` means the QTL would explain 5% of single-plot phenotypic
variance in a biparental RIL population; the background is polygenic with a
plot-basis heritability of 0.5. Run it on 50 paired replicate seeds:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
single <- fit_resamples(ril, sim_replicates(50))
```

```{r}
collect_metrics(single)
```

Power is the share of replicates in which the QTL was detected, here
`r round(collect_metrics(single)$mean[1], 2)` with a Monte Carlo standard
error of `r round(collect_metrics(single)$std_err[1], 2)`.
`location_error` is averaged over the replicates that detected the QTL (`n`
is smaller). `other_peaks` is the share of replicates with a significant peak
on another chromosome; with a polygenic background these are mostly real
background loci, not errors.

## Tune instead of loop

To ask how power depends on population size and the number of field
locations, and whether the answer changes with the size of the QTL, mark the
design arguments with `tune()` and put the assumption into scenarios. The
grid is crossed with the scenarios and every combination runs on the same
40 seeds:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ril_grid <- mapping_population(type = "RIL", lines = tune(), locations = tune(), generation = 6)

grid_res <- tune_grid(
  ril_grid,
  resamples = sim_replicates(40, scenarios = sim_scenarios(qtl_pve = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.08))),
  grid = expand.grid(lines = c(100, 200, 300, 400, 500), locations = 1:3),
  metrics = sim_metric_set(power, location_error, other_peaks, plots, cost)
)
```

```{r}
grid_res
```

That is `r nrow(grid_res$configs)` designs × `r nrow(attr(grid_res$resamples, "scenarios"))`
scenarios × `r nrow(grid_res$resamples)` replicates = `r nrow(grid_res$raw)`
simulated populations, with no loop written. The tidy summary has one row per
design, scenario and metric, with the usual tidymodels columns:

```{r}
collect_metrics(grid_res) |> subset(.metric == "power") |> head()
```

```{r power-curves, fig.alt = "Power against number of lines, one line per number of locations, one panel per QTL effect size."}
wide <- collect_metrics(grid_res, type = "wide")
ggplot(wide, aes(lines, power, colour = factor(locations))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = power - power_se, ymax = power + power_se), size = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  facet_wrap(~.scenario) +
  labs(x = "RIL lines", y = "Power", colour = "Locations") +
  theme_bw()
```

Because all designs share seeds, the curves are smooth even with 40
replicates: the same founders, QTL positions and field errors are drawn for
every design wherever the designs allow.

### Picking a design

`show_best()` and the `select_*()` helpers work as in tune, and accept
constraints. The cheapest design with at least 80% power for a QTL
explaining 5% of the variance:

```{r}
show_best(grid_res, metric = "cost", constraints = list(power = 0.8), scenario = "qtl_pve=0.05", n = 3)
```

and the design with the fewest plots whose power is within one standard error
of the best:

```{r}
select_by_one_std_err(grid_res, plots, metric = "power", scenario = "qtl_pve=0.05")
```

With the placeholder costs used here (US$15 a plot, US$20 to genotype a line
and US$2 per plant per single-seed-descent generation), a second or third
location is cheaper than the extra lines needed for the same power, because a
location adds only plots while a line adds plots, genotyping and nursery
work. Replace the costs with your own (`plot_cost`, `genotype_cost`,
`ssd_cost`, `cross_cost`) and the answer may change; that is the point of
making them arguments.

## Comparing population types

Population types take different arguments: RILs tune the filial generation,
BC*s*F*t* tunes backcrosses and generation, NAM tunes the number of families,
MAGIC the number of founders. A `sim_set()` holds one spec per type, each
with its own grid, and runs them all on the same seeds, like a workflow set.
Every design here has 300 lines in one location, so they use the same plots.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
common <- list(lines = 300L, qtl_pve = 0.05)
types <- sim_set(
  F2     = do.call(mapping_population, c(list(type = "F2"), common)),
  RIL    = do.call(mapping_population, c(list(type = "RIL", generation = tune()), common)),
  BCsFt  = do.call(mapping_population, c(list(type = "BCsFt", backcrosses = tune(), generation = tune()), common)),
  NAM    = do.call(mapping_population, c(list(type = "NAM", families = tune(), generation = 6L), common)),
  `AB-NAM` = do.call(mapping_population, c(list(type = "AB-NAM", families = tune(), backcrosses = tune(),
                                                  generation = 6L), common)),
  MAGIC  = do.call(mapping_population, c(list(type = "MAGIC", founders = tune(), generation = tune()), common))
)

types <- sim_map(
  types, "tune_grid",
  resamples = sim_replicates(40),
  grids = list(
    RIL      = data.frame(generation = c(3L, 4L, 6L, 8L)),
    BCsFt    = expand.grid(backcrosses = 1:2, generation = c(2L, 4L, 6L)),
    NAM      = data.frame(families = c(3L, 5L, 10L, 15L, 25L)),
    `AB-NAM` = expand.grid(families = c(5L, 10L, 15L), backcrosses = 1:2),
    MAGIC    = expand.grid(founders = c("4", "8"), generation = c(4L, 6L))
  ),
  metrics = sim_metric_set(power, location_error, support_interval, other_peaks, years, cost)
)
```

```{r}
types
ranked <- rank_results(types, "power")
ranked[, c("wflow_id", "rank", "parameters", "power", "power_se", "location_error", "years", "cost")]
```

```{r types-plot, fig.alt = "Power against cost for every design, coloured by population type."}
ggplot(ranked, aes(cost, power, colour = wflow_id)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = power - power_se, ymax = power + power_se)) +
  labs(x = "Cost (placeholder US$)", y = "Power", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

For detecting one biallelic QTL with 300 lines, a biparental population is
hard to beat:

* **RIL and BC1F*t*** lead. Later filial generations barely change power but
  shrink the location error, because more meioses break up linkage.
* **F2** (phenotyped as F2:3 family means) is the quickest, `r ranked$years[ranked$wflow_id == "F2"]`
  years to results, but has less power: the additive variance at the QTL in
  an F2 is half that in RILs.
* **Two backcrosses** lower power, since fewer lines carry the donor allele.
* **NAM and AB-NAM** lose power as families are added, because 300 lines
  spread over many families leave few lines per family and the QTL allele
  segregates only in the families whose donor carries it.
* **MAGIC** gives the narrowest location error of the multiparent designs but
  costs more here, since every line needs its own four- or eight-way cross.

This criterion counts only detection of one biallelic QTL. NAM and MAGIC are
usually chosen for what it leaves out: many alleles, a wider genetic base and
the chance to map several donors' alleles at once. A metric for those, added
with `sim_metric()`, would rank them differently; the study code would not
change.

## Racing: fewer simulations for the same answer

A wider search over lines (100–600) and generation (F3–F8) with 20
space-filling designs would take 800 simulations on 40 replicates.
`tune_race()` runs every design on 5 replicates, then drops designs that a
paired t-test says are worse than the leader, adding one replicate at a time:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ril_race <- mapping_population(type = "RIL", lines = tune(), generation = tune(), qtl_pve = 0.05)
params <- extract_parameter_set_dials(ril_race) |>
  update(lines = n_lines(c(100L, 600L)), generation = filial_generation(c(3L, 8L)))
race <- tune_race(ril_race, sim_replicates(40), grid = 20, param_info = params,
                  metrics = sim_metric_set(power, cost), burn_in = 5)
```

```{r race-plot, fig.alt = "Number of designs still in the race against replicates simulated.", fig.height = 3}
autoplot(race, type = "race")
show_best(race, n = 3)
```

The race used `r nrow(race$raw)` simulations instead of
`r nrow(race$configs) * nrow(race$resamples)`, and the survivors were run on
all 40 replicates, so their estimates are as good as a full grid's.

## Asking the question directly

Often the real question is "what is the cheapest design with at least 80%
power?". `tune_bayes()` answers it with a Gaussian-process search in which
expected improvement in cost is weighted by the modelled probability of
meeting the power constraint:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ril_cost <- mapping_population(type = "RIL", lines = tune(), locations = tune(), reps = tune(),
                               generation = 6, qtl_pve = 0.05)
params <- extract_parameter_set_dials(ril_cost) |>
  update(lines = n_lines(c(100L, 800L)), locations = n_locations(c(1L, 4L)), reps = n_reps(c(1L, 2L)))
bayes <- tune_bayes(ril_cost, sim_replicates(25), param_info = params,
                    metrics = sim_metric_set(cost, power, plots),
                    constraints = list(power = 0.8), initial = 8, iter = 15)
```

```{r}
show_best(bayes, metric = "cost", constraints = list(power = 0.8), n = 3)
```

```{r bayes-plot, fig.alt = "Cost against power for each design the Bayesian search tried, with the Pareto front highlighted."}
autoplot(bayes, type = "pareto", metric = c("cost", "power"))
```

It reached the same answer as the grid (about 300 lines at three locations)
after `r nrow(bayes$configs)` designs, without anyone choosing the grid.

## Scaling up

Everything above ran on a laptop-sized machine. For bigger studies:

* `control_sim(parallel = TRUE)` with `future::plan(future::multisession)`
  runs designs in parallel, on Windows too.
* `control_sim(cache = "cache-dir")` saves every finished replicate; rerun the
  same code after an interruption and only the missing replicates are simulated.
* `write_slurm_array()` writes Slurm scripts for SCINet Ceres or Atlas that
  split a `tune_grid()` across an array job and collect the results from the
  shared cache.

## What the simulator assumes

Results are only as good as the model. `mapping_population()` assumes inbred
founders with biallelic markers at 50% frequency, no crossover interference,
an additive trait (no dominance or epistasis), one target QTL plus a
polygenic background of `n_background` loci, and line means over locations
and reps with genotype-by-location variance. The MAGIC scan uses true founder
origin, so it is an upper bound on what haplotype reconstruction achieves.
See `?mapping_population` for every argument; each can be fixed, tuned, or
varied as a scenario.

In total this vignette summarizes `r format(n_sims, big.mark = ",")` simulated mapping populations.
